utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. May the registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. The case is IT-98-29/1-PT, the Prosecutor versus Dragomir Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Milosevic, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No microphone for the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, can you repeat yourself, please. And, Mr. Milosevic, you may be seated; you don't have to stand up. Can you answer me now, Mr. Milosevic. Can you understand the proceedings in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Although, the volume is too high up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Can you hear better now? Is that okay now, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. May we please have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Stefan Waespi, assisted by Manoj Sachdeva, John Docherty, and Jasmina Bosnjakovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Appearances for the Defence. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, everyone. Your Honour, my name is Branislav Tapuskovic, attorney-at-law, appearing on behalf of Mr. Dragomir Milosevic. With me is my co-counsel Branislava Isailovic, attorney-at-law from Paris.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tapuskovic. Thank you. Now, if we may move on to the reasons for the conference. This is a Status Conference which has been convened pursuant to Rule 65 bis of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The last Status Conference in this case was held on the 10th of July, 2006. According to the Rules, a Status Conference shall take place within 120 days of the last Status Conference to organise exchanges between the parties, to ensure an expeditious preparation for trial, to review the status of the accused's case, and to allow the accused an opportunity to raise issues in relation thereto, including his mental and physical condition. On the question of outstanding --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. It looks like there's no translation for Mr. Milosevic. Is there any ... The B/C/S booth, which side is it? Is it possible to get the technicians to help, or what could be done? Can we just try to say something to him and let's see if he hears.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic has confirmed that he's receiving interpretation in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We may now proceed. May we move on to the item called "Outstanding Motions." There are no pending motions at the present moment; am I correct? Will you confirm that, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you also do so, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In essence, I believe there are no major outstanding motions at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tapuskovic. Okay. Then the 65 ter filings. At the last Status Conference, the Defence declared that the translations of 424 exhibits had still not been provided to them, in particular, two witness statements which they claimed had already been translated and were available to be provided to them. The Prosecution suggested that the Defence counsel should, themselves, submit these documents for translation. The Pre-Trial Judge requested that the Prosecution check for the two particular witness statements and take responsibility for submitting the other documents for translation in order to assist the Defence. The question is: What progress has been made on the status of this issue, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Yes, indeed, at the last Status Conference, David Akerson undertook the obligation to initiate the proceedings to translate these famous 424 documents. We did so and we are pleased to announce that, at the end of this month, these 424 documents will be available in B/C/S. In relation to the witness statements, I understand, from reading the transcripts, that there are in fact six witnesses, and four witnesses were named specifically by Mr. Tapuskovic with numbers. And that's on page 174 of the transcript of the last Status Conference. And in the meantime, we checked our records and we did disclose what we thought were these six remaining witness statements in both languages, English and B/C/S. And we will be meeting after the Status Conference, and the Defence can confirm to us that this, indeed, happened. So, in our perspective, we complied with the undertaking we did last time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Waespi. Mr. Tapuskovic, can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I must raise this issue yesterday again, this first question pertaining to translation. I am very satisfied, as counsel for Dragomir Milosevic, that we can receive these 400-plus documents by the end of the month so that we could forward them to Dragomir Milosevic himself, after which we, of course, expect certain comments and suggestions on his part, without which we cannot work. We all know what is foreseen by Rule 66 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, but when it comes to translations, I always used the Statute as my benchmark, since this has precedence over the Rules. And Judge Antonetti, on the 12th of December last year, stated that Article 21, paragraph 4(A), of the Statute needs to be respected; this being that the accused can be notified in a timely fashion and as regards the reason for the indictment against him in a language he understands. So not only testimonies or statements, but rather all the documentation needs to be translated to the language of the accused so that he can provide comments to his Defence. In principle, therefore, I need to insist on that rule and that article. As regards the statements we are discussing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards the statements, I can confirm, Your Honour, that we have received a notification a few days ago, according to which the names of the witnesses have been identified, the names of the witnesses that were disclosed to us. However, three witnesses are outstanding; these are 033, 046, and 111. Also, there is another witness whose statement has not been disclosed to us. According to our information, this is witness number 4. And a few statements of Bosnian citizens. However, I believe that we will be able to resolve this during the meeting we are going to have with the Prosecutor so as not to take up too much of your time here. For the moment, I believe this should suffice to address the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tapuskovic, I'm a little concerned that it looks like, in what you said, you're confusing 65 ter filings with 66(A) filings, and I would like us to try and separate these two so that we deal with them separately. Can you very briefly, maybe in just one word, confirm what Mr. Waespi said in relation to the 65 ter filings; in other words, the 424 exhibits that he says you will be able to get within the next few days, by the end of the month, and the translation of some of those statements. You confirm that, what he said?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Everything I said concerns the list according to the 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now let's, then, move to the Rule 66 disclosures. At the last Status Conference, the Defence declared that it was still missing six witness statements. Now, I think you probably have covered them already in what you said, Mr. Tapuskovic. Anyway, the parties then agreed to meet after the Status Conference to determine which documents were missing and to resolve that dispute, okay? The Trial Chamber has been copied on correspondence from the Prosecution, letters dated the 16th of October and the 26th of October, 2006, in which the Defence was informed of the identities of a number of witnesses and provided with their statements. You have actually referred to them now, as you spoke, and you have mentioned that witnesses W033, W046, and W111 are still outstanding. In the correspondence, I note that the Prosecution concedes that and they undertaken, as soon as possible, to provide you with those witness statements. Are there any -- barring those three, are there any Rule 66(A)(i) and (ii) matters which remain outstanding. From you, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. One big issue is the Defence request of, originally, last November and confirmed in a letter of 24th March of this year. In this request, the Defence wanted many, many documents that relate to paramilitaries that were active in Sarajevo during the relevant time, and the Defence gave us search criteria and the OTP conducted these huge searches. Again, we are pleased to announce that we were informed by our technical people that these searches are available and will be put on case-specific EDS to be picked up by the Defence. But I have to tell you that these are -- that's an amazing amount of data that's being made available to the Defence, and we are told -- I think it's a range of, I think, 12 gigabytes, or something, amounting to, I believe, more than 12.000 documents. But, again, that's being done according to the wishes of the Defence and they can -- you know, it's made available to them. A number of people from the OTP have assisted the technical people from the Tribunal. I remember that three people worked 100 per cent during one month to put together this disclosure. So, as I said before, it will be made available to the Defence in the next few days, these 12.000. There are other parts of this huge request by the Defence which are witness statements and Rule 70 materials. These, obviously - I'm sure you understand, Your Honour, and the Defence - cannot be put to the Defence as such. So we from the OTP have to individually look at these searches and maybe make it available to the Defence, perhaps in a more specific way. For instance, they could come to our offices and perhaps sit on a computer and inspect it, as the Rule 66(B) says. So, in short, we have finished with these 12.000 which -- documents which can be given to Defence; and the second part, and that's, I think, about 8 or 9.000 documents, we can talk to the Defence how we actually proceed in relation to those. So we are making a lot of progress on this, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just ask, before you sit down, Mr. Waespi, are these documents Rule 66 kinds of documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I looked at the correspondence, Your Honour, and the Defence had labelled it under Rule 68, what they considered to be exculpatory. In a way, it's a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you say the Defence had labelled it or the Prosecution had labelled it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, the Defence had labelled it under Rule 68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, in a certain sense, it's a specific request coming from the Defence under 66(B). I don't think it's important to distinguish that because most documents are, anyway, in a language the Defence and the accused will understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Mr. Tapuskovic, you confirm? We're dealing with disclosures in terms of Rule 66(A)(i) and (ii).

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot confirm this. We asked for the documents my learned friend has mentioned, but we didn't discuss whether this was under Rule 66 or 68. We never stipulated that. We know that such documentation is in existence, but we cannot know whether they fall under Rule 66 or 68 before we are able to see them. We wanted to see everything they have on paramilitary activities, but we don't know what rule it falls under.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you there, Mr. Tapuskovic; I'm very sorry to do so. Mr. Waespi indicates that the documentation, in any case, is in B/C/S, so that for your purposes it should be okay, irrespective of what label it goes under. It will be in a language that the accused understands. It will be coming. So even if you dispute that you had labelled the request as a 68 request, that doesn't really matter, okay? That resolves the issue; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you then accept that you will be getting these documents - I beg your pardon - in the next few days? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Anything else you would like to raise under Rule 66? Your co-counsel --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague will do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We have something that could relate to Rule 66 or 68, whatever the number of the rule. The problem is as follows: The documents made available to the Defence through the electronic system are very difficult for us to consult, for the team of the Defence, since most of the members of our team are in Belgrade. I raised the issue with the Prosecutor. Therefore, for us to consult these documents through this electronic system is something that is extremely difficult or even impossible, if we do it from Belgrade. So, personally speaking, I'm in Paris, so I can avail myself of that opportunity, can use the system. Therefore, even if I'm not a case manager in this case, I can look at the documents. But for Mr. Tapuskovic, it's impossible to do so. So it's as if the documents had not been disclosed at all to us. Therefore, that's an issue I would like to raise with the Prosecutor during our meeting. I've prepared a list of the documents and I'm going to ask for these documents to be disclosed in the classical manner, in hard copy, for my co-counsel to be able to have a look at these documents. I'm going to prepare a list of selected documents; it's a shorter list. So the EDS problem is still there; it has not been resolved yet. I'd like to raise this matter with you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Isailovic. If I might just ask, what actually is the problem that makes it impossible for Mr. Tapuskovic, in Belgrade, to read documents in electronic form?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Let me give you a quick explanation. The problem is that the providers, the internet providers, in Belgrade provide only very slow communication, so the lines are extremely slow, and if you use the electronic system it takes forever. It takes so long that you cannot really conduct any decent research. And I can tell you about it because I tried, myself, using the system in Belgrade. If you want to conduct a simple research to obtain a small number of specific documents, it might take you hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you have any comment to make on that, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think the important issue is that, as you say, Mr. President, the Defence becomes used to that. And this is more for these bigger requests they made, like these 12.000 documents. There is no way these 12.000 documents can be made available in any other form than on the EDS. So we have to address that, and I'm sure we can do that. But in the past times, the Prosecution has always disclosed issues, for instance, just this week, on CD and DVD. We made quite a number of items available to the Defence, and they are being shipped to -- in fact, to Mr. Tapuskovic in Belgrade. And I take it that Mr. Tapuskovic and his assistants are able to open these CDs and work with those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just to interrupt. I didn't want to expose my ignorance in computers, but I would have thought that if it's provided in CD or DVD form, you don't need the internet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And therefore, the research can be done very quickly, as fast as the CD is able to play. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. You're entirely right. That's what we want; that's what we asked for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fine. Then Mr. Waespi says you'll get that. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are not asking anything more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That then disposes of that item, I believe. The next item would then be the Rule 68 disclosure. At the last conference the Defence again raised the issue that all documents submitted to them by the Prosecution had been submitted under both Rule 66 and Rule 68. The Defence claimed that this posed problems in distinguishing which material the Prosecution considers to be exculpatory. The Prosecution contested this, arguing that some material has been disclosed specifically as Rule 68. The parties were ordered to confer after the Status Conference to sort this matter out, and the Trial Chamber would like to -- well, the Pre-Trial Chamber would like to find out what the status is. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Indeed, since the last Status Conference, we have been disclosing materials exclusively under Rule 68, where we were sure that these documents or witness statements are exclusive under Rule 68. But there are a number of items which, in our assessment, relate to both incriminatory and exculpatory, and there, obviously, we say it affects both rules. So wherever we can say that it's exclusively Rule 68, we continue to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tapuskovic, any point?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What my learned friend, the Prosecutor, has said is quite correct. We have now set this course and I believe that we will continue to proceed along these lines in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tapuskovic. I would imagine, then, that this was the Rule 68 disclosure material issue. Can we then move to the question of agreed facts. At the last conference, the Prosecution requested expedited action by the Defence on the Prosecution's proposal of a list of potentially non-disputed facts filed on the 10th of May, 2006. The Defence submitted that they would move expeditiously on this issue, to the best of their ability, but did not provide a specific date by which they would respond -- when they would respond. The parties agreed to confer after the Status Conference to resolve the issue. What progress has been made in this matter, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The parties, indeed, met after the last Status Conference -- I'm not sure, though, what progress has been made. According to our correspondence, I believe that the ball is in the court of the Defence. So rather than try to summarise what I believe the status is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe, before you sit down, you can tell us whether you have had any response from the Defence to agree or disagree with your proposed list of agreed facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I don't think so, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It looks, then, from what you say, like the situation is where we were at the last Status Conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. And I believe Mr. Tapuskovic explained well the position he finds himself in, in dealing with this issue, and I believe he also linked it to the translation of these important documents, these famous 424 documents, which allows him and, indeed, his client to look more in an informed fashion at the proposal of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, it's true, we are faced with the problem of the translation of these documents, but this problem is going to be resolved very soon, as we know. But, on the other hand, during the meeting we had after the conference, we were told that the indictment might be amended. We took note of this information, and we are still expecting for this amendment of the indictment. On the other hand, in our pre-trial brief of the 27th of February, 2006, we tried to shed some light on a number of issues and to accept some of the facts submitted in the pre-trial brief of the Prosecution. And we are not only talking about facts that we accepted, but we also accepted the application of the law that, during the Galic trial, had been the object of a number of -- a discussion that had been very much discussed and challenged. Therefore, when it came to the application of the Geneva Protocols, we accepted, we, as a Defence team, accepted the application of the Geneva Protocols. Therefore, I believe that we have come a long way. We have accepted a great deal of what is stated in the indictment and in the further submissions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you have any disputes with that, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, that's correct, what the Defence said. They have acknowledged a few points in their pre-trial brief, and we are very grateful for that. In relation to the proposed amended indictment, I was waiting for an opportunity, according to your agenda, to address you, Mr. President, and I can do that at any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. To the extent that the amended indictment is relevant to the issue at hand, maybe you could address the Chamber, but I can understand that if the intention is to amend the indictment, then there's no way of -- we can talk about agreed facts because we don't know what the indictment is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. On the other hand, as I will explain later, the indictment is nothing new. There are no new charges, no new counts. It's just a little bit in a different format. It adds a few issues, but it -- I don't think it affects the Defence's ability to agree. There is more, though, on the background, the career, of the accused, which we hope, of course, the Defence might agree to. So in that sense, I believe the Defence is right to perhaps wait a little bit until the proposed amended indictment indeed has been accepted by the Trial Chamber, which is, of course, the next step.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: However, there is still the point of the proposed list by the Prosecution. There must be a set of facts which, I would imagine, it should be possible for the Defence to either admit or deny, irrespective of whether or not they have an amended indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, that's correct. It's, I believe, 40 pages of facts. And we are happy, ready, at any time, to sit down with the Defence. I take it that will be after the end of the November, when the Defence has received these 424 documents and has a chance to raise it with their client. So I guess December might be a good time to sit down and go over these 40 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Would it then be okay for the Chamber to order that the parties do sit down between now and the next Status Conference to resolve this issue? I see the Defence team is nodding their heads. I take it that means they agree. And I take that your nodding of the head, Mr. Waespi, also means that you agree. Thank you so much. We will then leave that matter on that basis. Are there any other matters that the parties would like to raise? That sort of bring us to the end of the matters that the Chamber wanted to raise. So any matters from your side, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The Prosecution, as you heard a moment ago, communicated to the Defence a couple weeks ago that we are in the process of amending the indictment. I would just like to briefly elaborate on the Prosecution's intent in this regard. The proposed amended indictment provides, in our belief, a more clear, precise, and succinct description of the Prosecution's case than the initial indictment, which dates back to 1999. This greater clarity will be of assistance to both Your Honours and the Defence and the accused. In conformity with case law of this Tribunal developed since the initial indictment was approved, as I said, in 1999, the proposed amended indictment also narrows down the modes of liability under which the accused has been charge and pleads with greater specificity material facts concerning the acts and conduct of the accused. The proposed indictment lays no new charges - I think that's very important, Your Honour - against the accused, nor does it contain any new allegations of fact. So it's really a new form but basically old content. So we believe that there is no delay in the proceedings. We can just go ahead as planned. We will be ready fairly soon, maybe in the next couple of days, and we'll, of course, Your Honour, ask for leave to amend the old indictment and the Defence has a chance to respond that. At the same time, perhaps a little bit later, we are also amending the -- proposing to amend the exhibit list. We are working hard on that. As you know, as the Defence knows, the OTP has been made available a large collection called "Banja Luka Collection," which contains important documents. In fact, they are called "SRK Archives" That's archives that contain documents relevant to the corps the accused had been leading. We have a team down there looking at these documents and they continue to do so. And the fruits of these documents, we propose, Mr. President, will be added to the exhibit list. There are other documents which came to our attention. Some of them we've had for a while and we have been consistently informing the Defence of the existence of these documents. Most of them are being disclosed, and we told the Defence specifically that we might be adding them to the exhibit list. The third motion which we are contemplating, Your Honour, is a motion to add witnesses; not many, but there are a few, also some related to these new documents; investigators who might provide, if necessary, information about the chain of custody of these documents; other witnesses whom we recently talked to whom we will ask leave, Mr. President, under Rule 66(A)(ii), the last sentence, to add to the original list of witnesses. At the same time, Mr. President, we are reviewing our original list of witnesses - I think there are 140 witnesses - and we will certainly be dropping witnesses from that list and we will inform the Defence, as soon as we decide to do so, about that so they can make their arrangements. So these are the three motions that will be forthcoming fairly soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Waespi. Mr. Tapuskovic, any comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm very glad that the Prosecution intends to make the indictment more concise and to make the work of all of us on the indictment much easier, meaning the Defence team and the accused, Dragomir Milosevic. But what I hear means that important searches are being conducted and we also, as the Defence team, are gathering our own evidence. But this means that the Prosecution still intends to carry out a substantial amount of investigative work, and so based on that we will have to adapt what we do. I am emphasising this because I believe we need to also pay attention to Article 20 of the Tribunal's Statute, which also calls for expeditious work. At this point in time, with all due respect, I must, in a way, kindly ask the Trial Chamber to do what it can on its part to speed up the entire procedure so that we at least have some idea of when the trial would be able to start, because in this situation, this is something that does need to be addressed. We do need to pay heed to Article 20 of the Statute. We are expecting an amended indictment, so we have to see -- I don't believe that we will have any objections, precisely for the reasons that I have mentioned. But I believe at this point in time this is a question that needs to be dealt with, the question as it relates to Article 20 of the Statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, Mr. Tapuskovic, are you asking that the Prosecution be put on terms? In other words, are you asking that the Prosecution be given deadlines by when they are supposed to do the outstanding things that they have been saying they will be doing? I would imagine that what is good for the goose would also be good for the gander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honour. We do need to take that into account, but it would be good to have some sort of deadline so that we could orient ourselves. At the moment we are working without any funding from the registry. We are receiving vast amounts of material, we are constantly on the road, so we are investing a lot of effort as it relates to exhibits and other things. So it would be good to know some kind of deadline, some sort of frameworks, within which the job can be completed; and also we need to take into account the provisions of Article 20 of the Statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to make specific proposals on the deadlines, on what issues you would like deadlines and by when you would like to have the deadline? Then we can put it to the Prosecution to find out whether they are able to meet that. Like, they've talked about amending the indictment, amending the exhibit list, and adding more witnesses to deal mainly with chain of custody and other things. Any specific suggestions you have on the deadline you would like placed on them?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am not in favour of rigorous deadlines, but I would like attention to be paid to all the matters that I have just raised so that we have some idea of when the proceedings will be able to start. I am not really advocating some sort of strict deadline that would make it more difficult for both of the sides to work, but I'm just making an appeal, with your help, to do as much as we can so that we can start with the trial as soon as possible. This is my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you happy with the time-lines suggested by Mr. Waespi that maybe by the end of November, when the Defence will have received the famous 424 documents, you will then have had an opportunity to discuss them with your client. And there would be some activity between -- during December between the parties by way of meetings, and hopefully by that time also the amendments will have been accomplished and you can sort them out, if they are not accomplished, in those meetings. And we can look forward maybe to the parties having resolved any outstanding issues by January 2007. Would that be a fair arrangement for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that that is an absolutely fair arrangement. I think that we ought to do our best to actually proceed as you have suggested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would that be fair to the Prosecution, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and I can commit ourselves to certainly filing the amended indictment and the motion to add exhibits within this month, but it will be earlier. Just in terms of adding exhibits, as you know, Mr. President, and as the Defence knows, that's a continuing exercise. We are certainly making mistakes; we might be missing some exhibits which we propose to add later. So we do our best to complete this adding of exhibits by now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then we're looking at sometime in January, then, to hear progress on these outstanding issues, okay? Thank you very much. Any other matter, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tapuskovic, any matters that the Defence would like to raise which have not been raised so far?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you very much. I think that we have dealt with all the key matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then, as a last matter, may I address myself to Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Milosevic, are there any issues you would like to raise relating to your state of health, both physically, mentally, emotionally, psychologically, and to your conditions of detention? Please remain seated. You may remain seated, Mr. -- you may sit down. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. Everything is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Everything is fine. With your health?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I know at the last Status Conference you told the Chamber that you enjoyed very good health. Is that still the case?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And are you happy with the conditions at the Detention Unit? Well, maybe "happy" is a wrong word. But you have no complaints to raise about the conditions at the Detention Unit?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, I have no objections, no complaints.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Chamber is quite pleased to hear that you have no complaints and that your health -- you are still enjoying good health. It doesn't look like there is any other matter at this stage, and so far as the Court is concerned, that brings us to the end of the pre-trial -- the Status Conference, I'm sorry. The matter will now stand adjourned. Court adjourned.
